name: Asenath
title: Joseph's Egyptian Wife
summary: Asnath, daughter of Potiphera, priest in the sun city of On (Heliopolis), belonged to the highest stratum of Egyptian society. When Pharaoh elevated Joseph to rule over all Egypt, he gave him Asnath as a wife—a union that solidified Joseph's position within the Egyptian power structure. Through her two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, Asnath had lasting significance for Israel's history. The patriarch Jacob adopted both sons and counted them as his own, granting them status as ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes. Asnath's role in the biblical narrative reveals the tension between Egyptian and Israelite identity, showing how God's plan of salvation extended beyond ethnic and cultural boundaries.

keyEvents.title: Marriage to Joseph
keyEvents.description: Pharaoh gave Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to Joseph as a wife as part of his elevation to ruler over all Egypt.

keyEvents.title: Mother of Manasseh
keyEvents.description: Asenath bore Joseph's firstborn son, Manasseh, before the famine struck. The name means 'God has made me forget' and refers to Joseph's earlier sufferings.

keyEvents.title: Mother of Ephraim
keyEvents.description: Asenath then bore to him and Joseph a second son, Ephraim, whose name means 'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.'

keyEvents.title: Her Sons Are Blessed by Jacob
keyEvents.description: Asenath's sons Manasseh and Ephraim were adopted by Jacob and received the patriarch's blessing, with the younger Ephraim placed before the older Manasseh.

versions.summary: Asenath was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), and was given to Joseph as a wife by Pharaoh himself. She became the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim, both of whom became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes. Through her, Joseph's descendants were integrated into both Egyptian and Israelite history.

versions.reason: [minor] The role 'matriarch' is somewhat imprecise for Asenath. She is not one of the traditional matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah), but she is the mother of two patriarchs. Adding 'wife' as a role gives a more complete picture.; [minor] Spelling error: 'Asnatts' should be 'Asnaths' or preferably 'Asenath' with an 'h' -> 'Asenath's'. Consistency with the title 'Asenath' requires that the genitive be written 'Asenath's'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could mention that she was of Egyptian origin and that this marriage marked Joseph's full integration into Egyptian society.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a profile like Asenath, there are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be covered, including information about the city of On/Heliopolis, the etymology of the name Asenath/Asnaths, and the apocryphal text 'Joseph and Asenath'.

versions.summary: Asenath was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), and was of prominent Egyptian origin. She was given to Joseph as a wife by Pharaoh in connection with his elevation to second-in-command over Egypt, marking Joseph's full integration into Egyptian society. She became the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim, both of whom were adopted by the patriarch Jacob and became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes. Through her, Joseph's descendants were integrated into both Egyptian and Israelite history.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good, but it closely resembles the previous version (v1). It should be rephrased more to provide fresh text and avoid repetition.; [minor] The role 'matriarch' can be debated – Asenath is not normally counted among the biblical matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah). A more precise role could be 'mother of Ephraim and Manasseh' or 'progenitress'. Nevertheless, it is not directly incorrect, but could be nuanced.; [minor] The phrasing 'Asenath bore Joseph his firstborn son Manasseh' is somewhat awkward. Better: 'Asenath bore Joseph's firstborn son, Manasseh'.; [minor] 'Asenath also bore her second son Ephraim' – it should be clarified that this is her and Joseph's second son. 'Her' is slightly ambiguous.; [minor] The dating of 'Joseph and Asenath' is debated. Many scholars date it to the 1st or 2nd century AD, not BC. It is safer to say 'from antiquity' or 'from the last centuries BC or the first centuries AD'.

versions.summary: Asnath, daughter of Potiphera, the high priest of the sun city On (Heliopolis), was a woman of high rank in Egyptian society. When Pharaoh elevated Joseph to vizier over all Egypt, he gave Asnath to him as wife – a political and social bond that solidified Joseph’s new position. As mother of Manasseh and Ephraim, Asnath held a decisive place in Israel’s history: her two sons were adopted by the patriarch Jacob and counted as his own, thus becoming ancestors of two of Israel’s twelve tribes. In this way, the figure of Asnath connects Egyptian and Israelite identity within the biblical narrative.

versions.reason: [minor] The term 'vizier' is an anachronistic designation originating from later Arabic/Ottoman administration. The biblical text does not use this title directly, although Joseph's role can functionally be compared to such a position. Consider using 'second-in-command' or 'administrator over all Egypt'.; [minor] Describing Potiphera as 'high priest' is an overinterpretation. The Hebrew text uses כהן (kohen), which means 'priest'. There is no basis for specifying that he was a 'high priest' rather than a priest of high rank.; [minor] In the event 'Her sons are blessed by Jacob', Asenath is not explicitly mentioned by name in all the cited verses. Verse 48:9 is relevant since Joseph mentions they are 'my sons whom God has given me here', but it may be worth including verse 48:13-14, which shows the actual blessing action where Ephraim is placed before Manasseh.

footnotes.text: On (Hebrew: און) was the biblical name for the Egyptian city of Heliopolis, one of the most important religious centers in ancient Egypt, known for its sun worship and connection to the sun god Ra. The fact that Asenath was the daughter of a priest there indicates she came from one of Egypt's most prominent religious families.

The name Asenath (Hebrew: אָסְנַת) is likely derived from the Egyptian ns-N.t, meaning 'belonging to (the goddess) Neith.' Neith was one of the oldest and most honored goddesses in ancient Egypt, especially in the Delta region. This underscores Asenath's deep roots in Egyptian culture and religion.

There exists an apocryphal Jewish text from antiquity known as 'Joseph and Asenath,' which tells an expanded story of Asenath's conversion from Egyptian idol worship to faith in the God of Israel before her marriage to Joseph. The text reflects early Jewish reflection on the challenges of mixed marriages and questions of identity.

Some rabbinic sources identify Potiphera with Potiphar, Joseph's former master, but this is disputed. The two names are linguistically related (both can mean 'the one given by Ra'), but most modern scholars treat them as two different individuals.

The fact that Joseph's sons by an Egyptian woman were incorporated among the tribes of Israel testifies to a remarkably inclusive attitude in the biblical tradition. Jacob's adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:5) gave them full tribal status on par with Jacob's own sons.

Archaeological findings from Heliopolis (Tell Hisn, near modern Cairo) confirm the city's role as an important religious center in the second millennium BCE. The temple of the sun god Ra-Atum was one of the largest in Egypt, and its priesthood wielded significant political and religious influence.
